messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
Amara is a twenty-year-old pharmacist who came to the United States with her family when she was twelve, but three years ago she returned to her country of origin for what was supposed to be a short visit. During that trip she was detained by armed men who accused her family of supporting opposition groups. For several days they kept her in a small concrete room with no windows. At various points they forced her head into a barrel of water until she lost consciousness, then dragged her back onto the floor, coughing and gasping. They screamed at her—endless arguments about things she did not know, demands she could not answer—and when she failed to give them what they wanted, they grabbed her wrists and made her kneel for hours, her arms twisted behind her back until her shoulders burned. She remembers fragments: the smell of mildew, the sound of a door sliding open, the weight of a hand on her neck. But whole sections of those days are missing, as though someone cut pieces out of a film. When she tries to tell her partner about it, the words vanish; she can only shake her head.

Now Amara works twelve-hour shifts at a chain pharmacy in a busy strip mall. Every morning she walks through the automatic doors and checks the layout for exits—the stockroom door, the employee bathroom window, the back delivery entrance. She never sits with her back to the store. When a customer raises their voice over a copay or a delayed prescription, Amara feels her chest lock and her palms go cold; she has to excuse herself to the break room, where she stands with her hands on the sink, watching the water run. She has stopped filling prescriptions that require her to draw up liquid from a vial because the motion of the syringe plunger makes her body stiffen, her shoulders hunch, her knees press together—the same position she held on that concrete floor, waiting for the next dunk.

She is in a relationship, and she loves her partner, but when they argue—even about something small, like forgetting to take out the trash—Amara’s mind goes blank and she hears only the raised voices from the room where she was held. She does not tell her partner this. She does not tell anyone. She is certain that if she starts thinking about what happened, the whole memory will flood her and she will not be able to function. So she pushes it down, keeps herself busy, works double shifts when she can. But at night, when she is alone in bed, she cannot let herself fall asleep. She has come to dread the moment her eyes get heavy, because in that drowsy drift she sees the barrel again, feels the hand on the back of her neck, hears the water sloshing. The nightmares—when they come—are so vivid she wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, convinced she is back in that room. To avoid them, she fights sleep as long as she can. She lies alert, listening to the furnace click on, the floorboards settle, her own heartbeat. She keeps the bedroom door open so she can hear the front door. She has to know she can get out. She has also stopped taking afternoon naps on her days off, because even a short doze on the couch can bring the same images rushing back. Instead she stays busy—cleaning, watching television with the volume high, anything to keep her mind awake until exhaustion finally pulls her under.

Over the months this vigilance has worn her down. She has started to believe she deserves to feel this way. Other people in that room did not survive, and she does not understand why she did. She tells herself, silently, that the exhaustion and the fear are exactly what she should carry. When she sees someone on the street who resembles one of the men—same height, same jacket, same way of walking—she crosses the street or ducks into a shop. She has stopped going to the park near her apartment because there is a large decorative pond, and even the sight of still water makes her stomach turn.

What finally brought Amara to the clinic was a moment at work last week. A teenager dropped a full cup of soda near the register; the liquid spread across the tile and Amara froze, her body locking into that old posture, her hands numb. A coworker touched her shoulder and she flinched so hard she knocked over a display. She could not explain herself. She went home early and cried for an hour, then called a number her partner had left on the kitchen counter weeks ago. She is afraid that telling the story will break something open inside her and she will never get it closed again. But she is also afraid of how small her life has become—how many places she avoids, how many arguments she walks away from, how tired she is of scanning every room before she can breathe.
